1What the Riemann Hypothesis says

A single vertical line is supposed to contain every nontrivial zero of a function built from all the positive integers. Why should estimates for primes have anything to say about a point in the complex plane?

1.1Follow one possible zero through the proof

Suppose, for the sake of following the argument, that ζ had a nontrivial zero ρ with real part 0.60. What would force a contradiction? Start with the zero, then work backwards to the arithmetic estimate needed to exclude it. The number 0.60 is an illustrative choice.

  1. A zero leaves a pole. Near a zero of multiplicity m, write ζ(s)=(s−ρ)mh(s), with h(ρ)≠0. Its logarithmic derivative therefore contains m/(s−ρ). The proof recovers this pole by integrating a function of prime powers against x−s−1. The function uses a ramp weight and subtracts an explicit main term. The arithmetic construction also introduces Dirichlet characters. When those are grouped, the multiplicities at the same zero have positive weights, so the pole survives. Compute its residue.
  2. A bound on distant intervals would exclude this pole. Choose a real exponent strictly between ½ and 0.60, for example 0.55. The analytic theorem excludes poles to its right if the real centered family sum is bounded above by a constant times x0.55 on arbitrarily distant intervals of the prescribed relative width. First fix a level whose weighted character sum sees the proposed zero. For each sufficiently small positive ε the arithmetic construction supplies auxiliary data giving windows for that same sum. Its exponent on the specialized route is ½+9ε. Taking ε ≤ 0.005, subject also to the construction’s threshold, puts the exponent at most 0.545. An exponent of 0.65 would leave a pole at 0.60 outside the reach of the theorem. The full argument makes this choice after the prospective zero. See the quantifiers.
  3. The interval comes from arithmetic. A prime-power count has two descriptions. Characters express its remainder in terms of centered sums. Maps between arithmetic lattices constrain the same count through divisibility at finite primes and size at the infinite places. Matching their main terms makes the residual error small enough. The length of a chain of theta lifts balances costs of size x/m and m. Cohomology supplies intervals where additional errors can be controlled at the same time. Follow the division by the total weight or see why the intervals coincide.

The contradiction rules out the proposed 0.60. Repeating it for every real part above ½ and using the functional equation excludes the other side of the strip. For characters the functional equation changes which character occurs. Follow the reflection step.

For a first reading, the prime-power calculation, the window theorem and reflection explain exactly what the arithmetic must deliver. Chapters 3–8 build that estimate and identify the deeper inputs whose explanations are still being developed. The reconstruction record gives their current scope.

1.2From a series to a function

Write s = σ + it, where σ and t are real and i² = −1. In the half-plane σ > 1 the sum ζ(s) = ∑n≥1 exp(−s log n) converges absolutely, since the absolute values sum to ∑ n−σ. Multiplying the geometric series in p−s over primes lists each integer exactly once by unique factorization. This gives the Euler product. For example, multiply just the factors for 2 and 3. The term from the second power of 2 and the first power of 3 is 12−s. No other choice gives 12. Absolute convergence allows the finite prime sets to increase until every integer appears. DLMF §25.2[1]

ζ(s) = ∑n≥1 n−s = ∏p prime (1 − p−s)−1   (Re s > 1).

Could the infinite product vanish although every factor is nonzero? This can happen for products in general. Here the logarithms are absolutely summable. For σ > 1 their absolute sum is at most ∑p ∑j≥1 p−jσ/j ≤ (1 − 2−σ)−1 ∑n≥2 n−σ. Exponentiating the convergent sum of logarithms gives a nonzero product.

At s = ¾ the original series is a divergent sum of positive terms. The expression ζ(¾) nevertheless has a precise meaning. There is a unique meromorphic function on the plane agreeing with the series throughout Re s > 1. Meromorphic means holomorphic except at isolated poles. Here the sole pole is at 1, and the continued function is regular at ¾. It is this continued function that the theorem studies. DLMF §25.2, definition and continuation[1]

1.3Which zeros?

The zeros at −2, −4, −6, … are called trivial. The remaining zeros lie in the strip 0 < σ < 1. Reflection pairs zeros across the line σ = ½. A pair at σ = 0.4 and σ = 0.6 would respect this symmetry, so symmetry alone leaves the main question open. DLMF §25.10(i)[2]

If ζ(s) = 0, s ≠ 1 and s ∉ {−2, −4, −6, …}, then Re s = ½.

This is Mathlib’s proposition RiemannHypothesis. A Lean function from complex numbers to complex numbers has a value at every input. Ordinary assertions about a meromorphic function at its pole concern a punctured neighborhood. The explicit exception at 1 lets us read the theorem in that ordinary sense. At zero the value ζ(0) = −½ eliminates another possible endpoint. Two public zeta theorems[3]

1.4Why the book follows characters

A Dirichlet character modulo a positive integer N is a multiplicative character on its invertible residue classes, extended by zero on nonunits. Its values on units are roots of unity. Inserting χ(n) in the series for ζ weights each residue class by a phase. The resulting function L(s,χ) agrees with ζ when N = 1. The principal character at a larger modulus drops all integers with a common factor with that modulus. For example at modulus 2 its series is (1 − 2−s)ζ(s) for σ > 1.

The proof first obtains right-half-plane nonvanishing for every χ and every nonzero modulus. Formally, σ > ½ and (χ ≠ 1 or s ≠ 1) imply L(s,χ) ≠ 0. Fixing the modulus-one character gives right-half-plane nonvanishing for ζ. The functional equation deals with the other side. The hard part is producing the prime-sum inequalities that lead to this nonvanishing. Character averages enter those inequalities before the specialization to ζ. Exact scopes[4] Proof bodies[5]

Check the role of modulus one

What can be concluded at a hypothetical point ρ with Re ρ = ¾ and ζ(ρ) = 0? Take N = 1 and its unique character. Then L(ρ,χ) = ζ(ρ), and ρ ≠ 1 follows from its real part. The character nonvanishing theorem contradicts this zero. At Re ρ = ¼ the same substitution does not meet the right-half-plane hypothesis. The reflection chapter constructs a point with real part ¾ to which it can be applied.

Read the source correspondence

RiemannZetaZerosOnLine names a proposition. riemannZeta_eq_zero_re proves it. The proof expression for both public zeta theorems is rhOfAll. It invokes Formalism.VW.rh_of_every allChi, which specializes the character and invokes Formalism.VW.rh_of_right. The separate theorem Claim.zeta also concludes a zeta statement. Its existence does not put it on this particular source route. Specialization[6]

To see what the arithmetic side must control, start with one prime power. Its weight is simple enough to integrate exactly. The next chapter follows that calculation all the way to a pole at a hypothetical zero.

2Prime powers and the Mellin transform

A prime contributes once to an Euler product, but contributes at every one of its powers to the logarithmic derivative. Follow the contribution from one prime power through a weighted sum and an integral. At the end, the multiplicity of a zero can be read from a single coefficient.

2.1How a prime power enters the sum

Write p for a prime. The von Mangoldt function Λ assigns log p to each positive power of p and zero to every other positive integer, including 1. Thus Λ(8) = log 2, while Λ(6) = 0. All logarithms here are natural. A Dirichlet character χ of modulus N ≥ 1 is a homomorphism from the multiplicative group of invertible residue classes modulo N to the nonzero complex numbers, extended periodically to the integers and set to zero on the nonunits. Its nonzero values are roots of unity because the group is finite. The principal character takes the value 1 on every unit. At modulus one the unique character takes the value 1 on every integer.

For real x ≥ 1, write t+ = max(t, 0). The smoothed sum is

Sχ(x)=∑n=1⌊x⌋Λ(n)χ(n)(xn−1)+(2.1)

The contribution from n begins at zero when x = n. After that point its slope is Λ(n)χ(n)/n. This gives a continuous, piecewise linear function on every bounded interval. The ordinary weighted count of prime powers would jump by Λ(n)χ(n) at n. The slope and the continuity here determine the two factors that will appear in the transform.

At x = 6. For the modulus-one character the active prime powers are 2, 3, 4 and 5. Their respective weights are 2, 1, 1/2 and 1/5. The sum is (5/2) log 2 + log 3 + (1/5) log 5. For the nonprincipal character modulo 3, the values on residues 0, 1 and 2 are 0, 1 and −1. In the same order the four terms now have character factors −1, 0, 1 and −1. The sum becomes −(3/2) log 2 − (1/5) log 5. Characters can remove a contribution, change its sign, or for a complex character rotate it.

Lean correspondence

The source defines Deduction.ramp for any function on natural numbers. Its finite range starts at 0. The formal summand there vanishes because Λ(0) = 0. The positive indices give (2.1) without requiring a division by zero. CharFamily, lines 8–19[7]

2.2The transform of one ramp

Set s = σ + it, where σ and t are real, and define xs = exp(s log x) for x > 0. We use the Mellin convention ℳf(s) = ∫1∞ f(x) x−s−1 dx. With u = log x, the measure dx/x becomes du and x−s becomes exp(−su). The transform therefore studies growth on multiplicative scales as an ordinary Laplace transform in u.

One-ramp identity. Let n ≥ 1 be an integer and σ > 1. Then

∫1∞(xn−1)+x−s−1dx=n−ss(s−1)(2.2)

The integrand vanishes up to n. Above n it is the difference of x−s/n and x−s−1. Both are absolutely integrable since σ > 1. Their integrals over [n, ∞) are n−s/(s − 1) and n−s/s respectively, by evaluating the power antiderivatives at the endpoints. Subtracting gives (2.2). At s = 2 and n = 2, the two areas are 1/4 and 1/8, leaving 1/8.

The half-plane matters. For large x, the absolute value of the integrand is asymptotic to x−σ/n. The integral of its absolute value diverges for σ ≤ 1. The formula on the right continues meromorphically beyond the integration domain. In particular a later evaluation of its continuation in the critical strip does not assert convergence of this integral there.

Lean correspondence

Deduction.mellin_ramp, statement and proof[8] removes the zero interval, rewrites the integrand and then integrates the two powers. The declaration uses Ioi 1, the open ray (1, ∞). Changing the endpoint value does not affect the integral.

2.3From one ramp to a logarithmic derivative

For σ > 1 define the Dirichlet L-function by the absolutely convergent series L(s, χ) = ∑n≥1 χ(n)n−s. Expanding geometric series at finitely many primes counts each integer supported on those primes exactly once. Letting the finite set grow gives the Euler product ∏p(1 − χ(p)p−s)−1, by absolute convergence. Its logarithm may be taken as the convergent series ∑p,j≥1 χ(p)jp−js/j, with p running over primes. Exponentiating recovers the product and shows it is nonzero there. NIST DLMF §25.15(i), equations 1–2[9].

Differentiate this logarithm with respect to s. The derivative of p−js supplies −j log p, cancelling j in the denominator. On every closed half-plane σ ≥ 1 + h, h > 0, the sum of absolute derivative bounds is at most ∑n≥2(log n)n−1−h < ∞ by the integral test. The differentiated series converges locally uniformly. Writing Dχ(s) = L′(s, χ)/L(s, χ), we obtain

−Dχ(s)=∑n=1∞Λ(n)χ(n)n−s(2.3)

To sum (2.2) under the integral, replace s by σ there. Since |χ(n)| ≤ 1 and the ramp is nonnegative, the sum of the integrated absolute values is bounded by

1σ(σ−1)∑n=1∞Λ(n)nσ<∞(2.4)

Indeed 0 ≤ Λ(n) ≤ log n for positive n. Fubini's theorem now permits the exchange of sum and integral. Equations (2.2) and (2.3) give the uncentered transform

ℳSχ(s)=−Dχ(s)s(s−1)(2.5)

Lean correspondence

The formal proof evaluates the integral norm at σ, sums it using absolute convergence, and replaces the Dirichlet series by its logarithmic derivative. The comparison with ∑(log n)n−σ is an elementary justification of that convergence in this exposition. Integral norm and exchange[10] identification of the logarithmic derivative[11]

2.4Why the correction terms have these signs

The raw transform has a factor 1/(s − 1). For ζ the logarithmic derivative has a pole at 1 as well. To detect zeros by their poles, we first remove the poles due to these main terms. This calculation only needs the primitive principal character (modulus one) and nonprincipal characters of positive modulus. A character is primitive if it is not induced from a character of any proper divisor of its modulus. The principal character at a higher modulus is induced from modulus one. The family used below excludes such higher-modulus principal characters.

A model for centering. A term of size xα has transform 1/(s − α) on Re s > α, by integrating xα−s−1. Subtracting this known term from a sum subtracts its pole from the transform. For example, x + x¾ has poles at 1 and ¾. Subtracting x leaves 1/(s − ¾), where the second pole is still visible. In the prime sum the known singularity at 1 includes a double pole, which calls for a second correction.

2.5The modulus-one case

Here L = ζ. Let γ = limk→∞(∑j=1k 1/j − log k), the Euler–Mascheroni constant. Put z = s − 1. The Laurent expansion ζ(1 + z) = 1/z + γ + O(z) gives an analytic function A(z) = zζ(1 + z) across 0 with A(0) = 1 and A′(0) = γ. Thus D1(1 + z) = −1/z + A′(z)/A(z) = −1/z + γ + O(z). Multiplying its negative by 1/[(1 + z)z] gives the principal part 1/z2 − (1 + γ)/z. NIST DLMF §25.2(ii), equations 4–5[12].

One coefficient is especially easy to miss here. The factor 1/[(1 + z)z] equals 1/z − 1 + O(z). When multiplied by 1/z − γ + O(z), the simple-pole coefficient receives −1 from the first factor and −γ from the second. Correcting only the double pole would leave a spurious pole with residue −(1 + γ).

Which functions of x have precisely these transforms? For Re z > 0, ∫0∞ exp(−zu) du = 1/z. Integration by parts, with u exp(−zu) vanishing at infinity, gives ∫0∞ u exp(−zu) du = 1/z2. Undo the substitution u = log x. These are the transforms of x and x log x. Hence set

G1(x)=S1(x)−xlogx+(1+γ)x(2.6)

For σ > 1 its transform is −D1(s)/[s(s − 1)] − 1/(s − 1)2 + (1 + γ)/(s − 1). The two negative-power coefficients cancel. The continuation is holomorphic at 1. This calculation uses the Laurent expansion around the pole and never substitutes a numerical value for ζ at its pole.

2.6The nonprincipal case

A nonprincipal character of positive modulus has an entire L-function, and the classical nonvanishing theorem at 1 gives L(1, χ) ≠ 0. Thus cχ = Dχ(1) is finite and Dχ(1 + z) = cχ + O(z). Equation (2.5) has principal part −cχ/z. Adding cχx to the sum cancels it. Analytic continuation[9] and the use of nonvanishing at one[13].

Gχ(x)=Sχ(x)+cχx(2.7)
ℳGχ(s)=scχ−Dχ(s)s(s−1)(2.8)

The numerator in (2.8) vanishes at s = 1. Dividing it by s − 1 leaves a holomorphic function there. This identifies the cancellation even when cχ happens to vanish. Neither centering formula estimates the size of the remaining error at large x.

Lean correspondence

The division in (2.8) is written with an overall minus sign in Deduction.mellin_Gchi_of_ne_one[14]. Its hypotheses are positive modulus, a nonprincipal character, and Re s > 1. Primitivity is unnecessary here. In Deduction.mellin_Gchi_modOne[15] the ζ correction is over a common denominator. The source extends (s − 1)ζ(s) to take the value 1 at s = 1 and identifies its derivative there as γ. Regularization at one[16]

2.7What a zero leaves in the transform

Let ρ lie in the strip 0 < Re ρ < 1, and suppose L(ρ, χ) = 0. The function is holomorphic near ρ and is not identically zero since its Euler product is nonzero for σ > 1. Its Taylor series has a first nonzero coefficient, of degree m ≥ 1. Factoring it gives L(s, χ) = (s − ρ)mh(s) with h holomorphic and h(ρ) ≠ 0. Differentiation and division give Dχ(s) = m/(s − ρ) + h′(s)/h(s). The last quotient is holomorphic on a sufficiently small disk about ρ.

Only the first term contributes a pole. In both centered formulas its multiplier is −1/[s(s − 1)], which is holomorphic at ρ since ρ differs from 0 and 1. Its value at ρ gives the coefficient of (s − ρ)−1, the residue of the continued transform Φχ.

Ress=ρΦχ=−mρ(ρ−1)(2.9)

A zero of any positive multiplicity therefore gives a simple pole. For ζ the factor s − 1 used to regularize it at 1 is a nonzero analytic factor at ρ, so the multiplicity here is unchanged.

Lean correspondence

Deduction.logDeriv_local[17] factors an analytic germ of finite order. Deduction.poleData_abstract[18] packages the local expansion. Deduction.poleData_char[19] constructs the continuation for a single admissible character. Lean records the Laurent expansion on a punctured neighborhood, so the totalized value assigned at a pole is immaterial.

2.8Why taking real parts preserves a pole

The arithmetic estimate later controls a real sum. Let I be a finite index set. For each i in I, let χi be a character of positive modulus Ni with Ni = 1 or χi nonprincipal, and fix a real weight ai > 0. Define GF(x) = ∑i∈I ai Re Gχᵢ(x). For a character χ, its inverse χ⁻¹ on units is its complex conjugate, and both characters vanish on nonunits. Conjugating the Dirichlet series first for σ > 1 gives L(s, χ⁻¹) = conj(L(conj(s), χ)) by analytic continuation. In particular the two derivatives and values at the real point 1 are conjugate for nonprincipal χ. The ramp has real weights. Therefore Gχ⁻¹(x) is the conjugate of Gχ(x), including in the modulus-one case.

Writing Re z = (z + conj(z))/2 before taking the transform gives the holomorphic expression ∑i(ai/2)(Φχᵢ(s) + Φχᵢ⁻¹(s)) away from its poles. Taking the real part of Φχ(s) would instead conjugate the complex integration kernel and lose this identity.

For a check on the complex variable, take a real function f(x) = 1 on [1,∞). Its transform is 1/s. At s = 2 + i this equals (2 − i)/5. Taking the real part after integration would discard the imaginary part even though the integrand’s input function was real. The transform of the character average keeps s fixed in both summands.

Fix a point ρ in the strip. Let mi and mi− be the orders at this same point of the functions for χi and its inverse, assigning order zero at a nonzero value. Set

B(ρ)=∑i∈Iai2(mi+mi−)(2.10)

The family has residue −B(ρ)/[ρ(ρ − 1)]. At a member of the formal zero set there is a witness i with a zero for χi at ρ or at its conjugate. The latter gives a zero for the inverse character at ρ. At least one order is then positive. Every other contribution is nonnegative in B(ρ), so the residue is nonzero. At real 0 < ρ < 1 it is positive because ρ(ρ − 1) < 0. This is the sign of a Laurent coefficient. The example modulo 3 already shows why signs of arithmetic summands require separate attention.

Strict positivity of the weights alone does not produce a pole. The abstract family may even have no indices. A pole requires the witness in the zero set. In the arithmetic application the retained set includes the modulus-one character. Its weight is 1. In the finite-group coordinates of the comparison, the comparison group is a product E0 × H. A retained character has weight 1 if it is trivial on the entire factor {0} × H, and 1/(3o + 1) otherwise, where o is the level parameter Λ.o. The averaging subgroup A0 can be smaller than H. Triviality on A0 suffices to survive averaging and does not by itself give unit weight. The factor 1/2 in (2.10) has the separate origin Re z = (z + conj(z))/2.

Lean correspondence

Deduction.CharFamily and Deduction.Gm[20] specify the weights and admissibility. Deduction.poleData, character pairs[21] constructs the family transform. Its residue and real-pole sign[22] use the zero-set witness. The level family[23] identifies the retained sum. Comparison of arithmetic weights[24] uses Deduction.CH.wtA[25].

2.9What the next theorem needs

In logarithmic coordinates set g(u) = GF(eu) for u ≥ 0. The packaged theorem Deduction.poleData uses a rough bound |g(u)| ≤ C e2u. To see why such a bound is available, each uncentered sum is bounded by x∑n≤x(log n)/n. Since (log n)/n ≤ 1, this is at most x2. On x ≥ 1 the correction terms are also bounded by a character-dependent constant times x2. Each ramp is continuous, and only finitely many contribute on every bounded interval, so the resulting g is measurable. A finite weighted sum preserves that bound. The corresponding formal proof is in Deduction.Gchi_growth[26].

This bound alone justifies absolute convergence of the Laplace integral in Re s > 2. The formal PoleData interface asks for the integral identity on this smaller half-plane, analyticity away from the zero set in Re s > 0, isolated poles there, and their nonzero residues with positive sign at real poles. The sharper Mellin identities above hold already in Re s > 1. Every point of Re s > 0, including a point outside the zero set, has a punctured neighborhood containing no family zeros. This follows by intersecting the finitely many zero-free punctured neighborhoods for the analytic members, using the regularized function in the modulus-one case. The modulus-one singularity at 1 has been removed explicitly. For the formal set defined using the totalized riemannZeta, the source also uses its assigned nonzero value at 1. Nonvanishing on the boundary[27]

The remaining task is to exclude a pole to the right of a chosen θ with 0 < θ < 1. The window argument accepts an upper bound on selected intervals, with gaps allowed. Precisely, fix δ > 0. For every η > 0 and starting threshold Y0, it needs some Y ≥ Y0 and a function R on [Y, Y1+δ] such that R ≥ 0, GF ≤ R there, and R(y)y−θ−1 is integrable on the interval with integral at most Yη. One can take the threshold at least 1. What this chapter supplies is the transform and its pole data. Obtaining these windows is an arithmetic problem. Showing that the windows force each pole to have real part at most θ takes a further analytic argument. Definition of the required windows[28] the theorem using them[29]

2.10Two checks on the argument

1. Suppose a weight is changed to (1 − n/x)+. Compute its single-term transform for Re s > 1. Where do the denominator factors move?

Show the calculation

On [n, ∞) subtract n∫ x−s−2 dx from ∫ x−s−1 dx. The result is n−s[1/s − 1/(s + 1)] = n−s/[s(s + 1)]. In fact this calculation works for Re s > 0. Using this weight in (2.2) would change both the denominator and the centering calculation.

2. Suppose χ is real and its L-function has a hypothetical zero of order three at a real ρ with 0 < ρ < 1. For a singleton family with weight 2, what is B(ρ)?

Show the calculation

The inverse equals χ because its nonzero values are real roots of unity. Both multiplicities in (2.10) are 3, so B(ρ) = (2/2)(3 + 3) = 6. The residue is 6/[ρ(1 − ρ)]. The two appearances of χ are compensated by the half in the real-part identity.

3From formal logarithms to divisibility

The proof needs a lower bound on the powers of p dividing derivatives of a theta kernel. A derivative becomes an entry of a linear map between lattices. Divisibility of those entries at many primes contributes to the global height estimate. The local difficulty already appears for one formal variable. Differentiation supplies a factorial, and undoing the formal logarithm introduces denominators. We can calculate both at the first degree where a denominator occurs.

3.1A height-two change of coordinate

The valuation vp(a) counts the powers of p in a nonzero rational a, allowing negative counts for denominators. Set vp(0) = +∞. The inequality v(a + b) ≥ min(v(a), v(b)) will carry estimates through finite coefficient sums. An integral series has coefficients of nonnegative valuation. In formal power series, questions about composition at zero can be answered degree by degree, without an analytic radius of convergence.

A formal group describes a group law by its power series near the identity. A formal logarithm converts its composition law into addition. Complex multiplication (CM) provides endomorphisms beyond integer multiplication. For a complex elliptic curve written as a quotient of the plane by a lattice, a CM scalar preserves that lattice. In the source the scalar is (1 + i√d)/2. At a suitable inert prime, the logarithm used for comparison has the following sparse shape. Put q = p².

ℓ(T) = ∑j≥0 Tqʲ/pj = T + Tp²/p + Tp⁴/p² + ⋯ .

Formalism.L2.Th1.CM.ltLog defines this series. The proposition CM3 specifies what the comparison has to deliver. It assumes squarefree d ≡ 3 mod 4, CM by this scalar, prime p ≥ 5 with p ∤ d, and no square root of −d modulo p. A good model and a field identification with the completed algebraic closure of ℚp are supplied. The conclusion gives a unit ε in the closed maximal unramified field such that all coefficients of the model’s series uSer composed with εℓ belong to that field and have norm at most one. The scalar and the direction of this composition matter. CM and its local field[30] Series and good-model assumptions[31]

3.2Proving the one-variable estimate

Here is an independent one-variable derivation of the loss. Take any characteristic-zero valued field extending the p-adic valuation, normalized by v(p) = 1. Since ℓ starts with T, it has a unique compositional inverse B with zero constant term and linear coefficient 1. Its coefficient bn satisfies

v(bn) ≥ −(n − 1)/(q − 1),   n ≥ 1.

Indeed B = T − ∑j≥1 Bqʲ/pj. To form degree n in a power with r = qj factors, choose positive indices summing to n. They are all smaller than n. Induction bounds their product after division by pj from below by −(n−r)/(q−1) − j. This is at least −(n−1)/(q−1) because 1 + q + ⋯ + qj−1 ≥ j. For fixed n only finitely many terms occur, and addition preserves the lower bound.

If A has integral coefficients, the degree-n coefficient of Br loses at most (n−r)/(q−1). For n ≥ 1 the constant term of A contributes nothing, so the same bound with r = 1 applies to A(B). Its n-th derivative at zero is n! times this coefficient. The exact factorial valuation is ∑j≥1⌊n/pj⌋. Each multiple of pj contributes one count at level j. Equivalently the sum is (n−sp(n))/(p−1), by expanding n in base p and summing each digit's geometric series. Since each digit is at most p−1, the deviation from n/(p−1) is at most 1 + logp n.

1/(p−1) − 1/(p²−1) = p/(p²−1) = p⁻¹ + p⁻³ + p⁻⁵ + ⋯ .

The first denominator at p = 5. Put q = 25 and choose the integral series A(T) = T. Up to degree 25, the inverse identity is B + B25/5 = T. As B starts with T, its 25th-power coefficient in degree 25 is 1. Hence [T25]B = −1/5. This attains the lower bound −(25−1)/(25−1) = −1. Its 25th derivative is −25!/5. The factorial has valuation ⌊25/5⌋ + ⌊25/25⌋ = 6, leaving valuation 5. This calculation isolates the inverse logarithm. The theta kernel also carries an exponential factor, whose mixed terms introduce the next loss.

3.3What mixed terms cost

In the multivariable estimate the derivative orders form a multi-index κ. The coefficient is multiplied by ∏i κi!. Set γp = p/(p²−1). With r coordinates and all κi ≤ a, a ≥ 1, the lower bound for the normalized valuation has the form

∑i κi(γp − σi) − r(logp a + 1).

What is a radius here? For the coefficient cν of a monomial Xν, assigning exponents ri measures its weighted valuation v(cν) + ∑νiri. A bound of zero means |cν|p ∏ |p|pνiri ≤ 1. The corresponding coordinate radius is |p|pri. Increasing ri shrinks that radius and makes the exponential easier to control. Recovering the unweighted coefficient of order κ then costs κiri. The baseline ri = 1/(p²−1) pays for the inverse logarithm. The extra σi is a choice. Weighted coefficient, integral series and factorial[32] threshold for exponentiation[33]

The exponential explains the target weight 1/(p−1). Write its exponent as F, with F(0) = 0. If every relevant monomial of F has weighted valuation at least 1/(p−1), a term in Fm/m! has weighted valuation at least m/(p−1) − vp(m!) ≥ 0. At a given derivative order κ only monomials componentwise at most κ can enter, and the zero constant term makes the coefficient sum finite. For a mixed monomial XipαXjpβ, the extra weight contributed by the chosen radii is pασi + pβσj. The proof shows that one extra valuation unit is sufficient for each pair failing the baseline test. This gives the inequalities that the optimization below has to satisfy. The monomial test and the exponential estimate[34]

The nonnegative corrections σi pay for mixed terms of an exponential factor. Each offending monomial with exponents pα and pβ at coordinates i,j within κ requires pασi + pβσj ≥ 1. Increasing either correction helps attain feasibility and reduces the final gain by κiσi or κjσj. The source first controls the series at radii 1/(p²−1), increases them by the corrections to control the exponential, multiplies the two bounds, and finally uses the factorial inequality. There are structural constraints on this optimization. The source assumes an odd prime, an even number of cyclic row labels ≥ 2, an ultrametric characteristic-zero field with ‖p‖ < 1, an unramified coefficient subfield, a specified primitive root, a series satisfying BHyp, and a row-respecting integral matrix. 3.4Choosing correction radii on a cycle

The correction attached to a coordinate has two parts to its construction. First assign one price σs to each row label s. Then adjust individual coordinates at the rows distinguished by the frame. The first problem has an exact optimum. For the adjustment, an explicit choice with a bounded total cost suffices.

Take integers p ≥ 3 and even d ≥ 2. The optimization itself imposes no primality condition on p. Labels belong to ℤ/dℤ. Give each label a real capacity Ds ≥ 0. For each odd integer 1 ≤ j < d, an amount xs,j ≥ 0 sent from s to s + j consumes pj units of capacity at its starting point and one unit at its endpoint per unit sent. Thus the load at s is ∑j (pjxs,j + xs−j,j). Require this load to be at most Ds. Write V for the largest total ∑s,j xs,j. The zero flow is feasible. After setting unused coordinates to zero, every used coordinate lies between 0 and ∑s Ds. The continuous objective therefore attains its maximum on a closed subset of a compact box. Variables, loads and objectives[39] Truncation and attainment[40]

A feasible price vector has 0 ≤ σs ≤ 1 and pjσs + σs+j ≥ 1 on every edge. Multiply each edge inequality by the amount sent, sum, and translate the index in the incoming sum. This gives ∑s,j xs,j ≤ ∑s σs load(s) ≤ ∑s Dsσs. Equality of the optimal values yields the gain used in the coefficient estimate, with γ = p/(p²−1). The weighted load identity[41]

F(D) = γ ∑s Ds − V = maxfeasible σ ∑s Ds(γ − σs).

To prove equality, let C consist of pairs (b,t) for which a nonnegative flow has load ≤ b in every row and value ≥ t. This is a convex cone. It is closed because for a converging sequence of pairs, their capacities stay bounded. Truncate the witnessing flows, take a convergent subsequence in a common box, and pass the load and value inequalities to the limit. For η > 0, the point (D,V + η) lies outside C. Strict separation gives a linear functional a·b + c t which is nonnegative on the cone and negative at that point. Independent positive capacity increments belong to the cone, so as ≥ 0. Since D ≥ 0 and V + η > 0, negativity forces c < 0. Test a unit flow on each edge. Its load and value give pjas + as+j + c ≥ 0. Dividing by −c supplies prices of cost < V + η. Closedness of the feasible cone[42] Separating functional and edge tests[43]

Clipping each price at 1 preserves every edge inequality. If either endpoint price was clipped, that endpoint alone now contributes at least 1 since pj ≥ 1. Clipping can only lower the cost because D ≥ 0. The feasible prices form a closed subset of the unit cube containing the all-ones vector, so the minimum exists. It is below V + η for every η > 0 and at least V by the load identity. Finally, every positive odd exponent j reduces modulo the even period d to another odd exponent r < d. The endpoint is unchanged and pjσs ≥ prσs. Thus the same optimizer satisfies the inequalities at all odd levels. For example, let p = 3, d = 2 and D = (1,1). Send ¼ along each of the two edges of length one. Each load is 3/4 + 1/4 = 1. The prices (¼,¼) attain equality on both edges and cost ½, proving V = ½ and F = 2(3/8) − ½ = ¼. If D = (0,1), both flows must vanish because both use the first row. The feasible prices (1,0) have zero cost. The formula still works with a zero capacity.

From an edge to a derivative. In the two-label optimization take p = 5, a single coordinate at each label, no distinguished rows, and derivative orders κ = (500,100). The edge from 0 to 1 represents the mixed exponent pattern X₀⁵X₁. Its constraint is 5σ₀ + σ₁ ≥ 1, hence 500σ₀ + 100σ₁ ≥ 100. The symmetric prices σ₀ = σ₁ = 1/6 satisfy both directed edges with equality. Equivalently, sending 100 along the first edge consumes exactly the capacities (500,100). The minimum cost is 100. With γ = 5/24 the leading gain is 600γ − 100 = 25.

One can check that choice directly on the coefficient in the source theorem. Suppose its series and frame hypotheses hold for this two-coordinate calculation. Including the baseline 1/24 gives weight 5/24 on each coordinate. A weighted valuation of at least zero permits an unweighted coefficient valuation as low as −600(5/24) = −125. The actual factorials contribute v₅(500!) = 100+20+4 = 124 and v₅(100!) = 20+4 = 24. The derivative therefore has valuation at least 23. The uniform estimate in the theorem gives the weaker 25 − 2(1 + log₅500) because it allows every coordinate order up to 500. The numbers in this example specialize the coefficient inequality. The kernel construction supplies its own diagram and frame. factorial times the weighted coefficient[47]

3.5From a row price to a coefficient bound

In the frame, a coordinate has label s, row index k < N0, and a further index below N1. At each distinguished label s in a set T, the coordinates with k = 0 form its top row. Their total derivative order is ν1(s). The remaining orders sum to Ds, which equals size(s) − ν1(s) on T and size(s) elsewhere. Assume 0 ≤ ν2 ≤ ν1 ≤ size. 3.6Transporting a theta function

A lattice is the integer span of linearly independent vectors in their real span. Its covolume measures one fundamental cell. A theta function on a complex vector space transforms by prescribed factors on translation by lattice points. That transformation law depends on a Hermitian form, so carrying a theta function between coordinate models requires control of both the lattice and the form.

One transport lemma takes the normalized function B.eNat on the space associated to two admitted lattices. A complex linear isomorphism e identifies their period lattice with S.La and preserves the Hermitian form. The source transports holomorphicity by composition with e−1. For a period x it pulls back the translation, uses integrality to write the real phase parameter as an integer m, and computes exp(πim) = (−1)m. The two translation laws then agree, including their sign. This step assumes the curve ideal, the nonzero twelfth-root normalization, the character, and the isometry. Its conclusion is membership in the target theta space. A global divisibility estimate still needs local coordinates, an integral expansion and a nonzero evaluated map. The transport lemma[66]

3.7Why iterating a lift requires more than a kernel

An automorphic function is, in this setting, a function on adelic group elements with the required invariance under rational group elements and additional regularity. A theta lift integrates a function against a special theta kernel to obtain a function on another group. Write Fk for a fundamental domain and νk for its ambient invariant measure. One permitted step from stage k has the form

fk+1(h) = ∫Fₖ Θk(g,h; Φ) fk(g) dνk(g).

The base function is smooth automorphic, square-integrable on the quotient, and belongs there to the prescribed starting subspace. At a step the test datum Φ must be admissible, and the integrand must be integrable for each h. The source spans the resulting functions. To meet a target subspace W it requires a member whose quotient class is outside W⊥. Even a well-defined sequence of operators can send a nonzero input to zero. This explains why a meeting or nonvanishing hypothesis is mathematically substantial. The chapter on theta lifts follows how a nonzero norm and the Hecke eigenspaces establish the meeting condition in the arithmetic chain. Nonvanishing along the lifts. 5Lattices and the arithmetic main term

A local valuation gain becomes a positive multiple of log p after taking a lattice height. The global argument compares the sum of those gains with a count of words in the theta construction. 5.1The lattices that carry the comparison

Over a number field K, an arithmetic lattice in a finite-dimensional K-vector space V is a finitely generated module over the ring of integers of K spanning V. To measure it one also needs norms at the infinite places. In the source a basis of V and a matrix Xv at each such place give these frames. The condition Good requires every frame to have nonzero determinant as well as finite generation and spanning. For a good lattice A of positive rank r over a totally complex number field, its mean slope is −(2/[K : ℚ]) log(ht(A))/r. Here ht is the source's lattice height in the chosen metric. The factor 2/[K : ℚ] averages over the complex places. A smaller height at fixed rank raises the mean slope. Think of a lattice through its finite list of Harder–Narasimhan slopes, each repeated according to rank. A step in its filtration contains the directions whose slopes meet a given threshold. The resulting list has arithmetic mean equal to the lattice's mean slope. For the source lattices subtract each height allowance and concatenate the lists over all words. Their mean is s and every entry is at most s + bF. If a fraction p lies below s − τ, for τ ≥ 0, then the mean is at most p(s − τ) + (1 − p)(s + bF). 6Theta lifts, local factors and the Galois input

How can a theorem attaching Galois representations in odd dimension give one in even dimension? Lift the same automorphic representation twice to a larger odd rank, adding different character lists each time. The shared part can then be recovered. Both global theta integrals must produce a nonzero form for this argument to start.

The iterated chain · Split and inert places · The finite test vector · Real places · Continuation · Inert cell calculation

6.1What is being lifted?

A Hermitian form measures lengths using both a field and its conjugation. On two complex coordinates the example is ⟨x,y⟩ = x₁y₁ + x₂y₂. Its unitary group consists of the changes of coordinates preserving this pairing. For a number field we can make such a change at each place. An adelic group element collects these choices, integral at almost every finite place. A rational change of coordinates gives the same change simultaneously in all completions.

An automorphic form here is a function on the adelic group, invariant under those rational changes on the left and satisfying additional finiteness and regularity conditions. Translating its argument on the right produces a space of functions carrying a group action. The irreducible space being lifted is U, and φ is one vector in it. A theta kernel converts φ into a function on another group by integration. To show that this conversion retains some information, one proves that a resulting vector has positive squared norm. At a good finite prime the commuting Hecke operators then provide a list of spectral parameters, with multiplicities, which can be compared on the two sides.

6.2Two parallel lifts to odd rank

Let E be a CM field, a totally imaginary quadratic extension of its totally real subfield F. The version used here assumes that E/F is unramified at all finite places, that E contains a square root of a negative rational integer, and that [F : ℚ] is even. At every nonsplit finite place the underlying prime of F has odd residue characteristic, norm greater than three and does not divide the absolute different of F. Take an even rank n ≥ 1 and an automorphic representation U of the definite unitary group of rank n. Fix its highest weights λ at the complex embeddings and a finite split place w₀ of E. Field and rank hypotheses[185] the two-lift statement[186]

For a Hermitian source with identity Gram matrix and signature (n, 0), the lifting theorem gives a rank threshold d₀. The proof chooses t = 2(d₀ + n) + 1. Both targets are definite skew-Hermitian models of rank D = n + t, an odd integer above the threshold. Each lift uses its own compatible pair of splitting Hecke characters. The proof takes a common lower bound b for the components of λ at the chosen complex embedding above each real place and chooses their target exponents so that mW,j(v) ≤ 2b − D. Thus every required archimedean inequality D + mW,j(v) ≤ 2λv,k holds. Applying the same rank theorem once for each pair produces U₁ and U₂. The rank theorem with its weight conditions[187] the construction and both applications[188]

There is one common algebraic Hecke character κ, and two lists ψj,h of t algebraic Hecke characters. No character from the first list equals any character from the second as a global character. At a split place w where κ and list j are unramified and U has a Satake multiset, write B(w) for its algebraically normalized eigenvalues. Unramified means the character is trivial on local units. Its value at a uniformizer is then well defined. The target eigenvalues obey the following multiset identity, with multiplicities retained.

Bj(w) = κ(w)−1B(w) ⊔ {ψj,h(w) ∣ 0 ≤ h < t}.

At infinity the target weight jumps are the union of the original jumps shifted by the weight of κ and the negatives of the weights of the added characters. At the chosen w₀ the construction specifically guarantees that κ and every member of list 1 are unramified. Distinct global characters can agree in value at an individual prime. The proof compares their associated global Galois characters. Normalized Satake parameters, weights and the chosen place[186]

6.3Why each global theta lift is nonzero

The lifting theorem first obtains a real threshold L for integrability of a height power against Haar measure. Taking an integer N > 2L and d₀ = max(N, 2n) gives both D ≥ 2n and L < D/2. For splitting characters with the prescribed restrictions and archimedean exponents, the real-place pairing supplies a nonzero vector f∞ in the Weil model and a nonzero automorphic form φ with matching type. The outstanding choice is the finite-place Schwartz vector ffin. Threshold and matching archimedean data[189]

Let ω be the Weil representation of the source and target adelic unitary groups on test functions on adelic n-by-D matrices over F. For a source group element g and a target element h, its theta kernel sums the translated test function over rational matrices, diagonally embedded into the adeles. With DX the model’s source integration domain, the lift of φ is the function of h given by

Θ(Φ, φ)(h) = ∫DX (∑ξ∈Matn×D(F) [ω(g, h)Φ](ξ)) φ(g) dμ(g).

This convention conjugates the source form. The matrix coefficient used to test nonvanishing pairs ω(g, 1)Φ with Φ using additive Haar measure on the adelic matrix space. I(Φ, φ) = ∫ cΦ(g) mφ(g) dg.

Choose a finite set S containing enough places to control the level of φ, the ramification and the tail estimate. Use a local bump vector at each place of S and the model's vacuum vector elsewhere. The proof decomposes the integral into archimedean, finite-in-S and outside-S factors. The Schur calculation supplies a nonzero scalar and the chosen coefficient is nonzero at the identity. 6.4Recovering the even-dimensional representation

To see the danger in subtracting eigenvalues at just one prime, take the cyclic group of order four generated by g. The two characters taking g to 1 and −1 agree at g². A list of values at g² cannot tell which character was added. Once two semisimple representations have been identified as representations of the entire group, one can compare the multiplicities of each irreducible constituent and subtract known character lines. The argument below explains how the good primes supply that global comparison.

Apply the available odd-rank Galois theorem twice, each time in dimension D. It attaches continuous semisimple ℓ-adic representations ρ₁ and ρ₂ to U₁ and U₂. Let χj,h be the ℓ-adic character attached to ψj,h, and Pj(g, X) the characteristic polynomial of ρj(g). Injectivity of the Hecke-to-Galois character map preserves disjointness across the two lists. Comparing normalized Frobenius data at good split places and using density gives, for every Galois element g,

P₁(g, X) ∏h(X − χ2,h(g)) = P₂(g, X) ∏h(X − χ1,h(g)).

The representations ρ₁ ⊕ ⨁χ2,h and ρ₂ ⊕ ⨁χ1,h consequently have the same characteristic polynomials. The source uses semisimplicity and a one-character splitting theorem to separate a line χ1,h from ρ₁ and retain a comparison identity for the complement. Induction removes all t lines, preserving continuity, semisimplicity and the required local conditions. The remaining dimension is D − t = n. Tensoring with the ℓ-adic character of κ restores the original normalization. Given a source Satake multiset at w₀, unramifiedness of the first list supplies the local conclusion there. Repeating the construction at each split place gives weakly compatible representations. Their isomorphism transports the local conclusions to a common representation. 6.5The row and its adjoint

An automorphic form is a function on an arithmetic quotient of a group with specified transformation and regularity properties. A theta lift uses an integral kernel to carry such functions between groups. In the part of the proof examined here, the relevant spaces of forms at fixed level and weight are presented as finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces. This allows a precise question about nonvanishing before any local representation is identified.

Fix an index i. It specifies a row number j and a tuple of character data μ. Suppress these two subscripts. Write M for the row space and V for the target space, called Mj j and Mt μ j in the source. There is a linear map P from V to M. Its adjoint T goes from M to V. The row space has designated subspaces Mσ for its types σ. A type here labels a component of the space of forms. The target has subspaces Vπ for target types π. Finite-dimensional spaces and downward operator[209] upward adjoint[210]

The required Gram hypothesis says that PT acts by a real scalar λσ on Mσ, strictly positive whenever Mσ is nonzero. For every f in that subspace the adjoint identity gives

‖Tf‖2 = Re ⟨f, PTf⟩ = λσ ‖f‖2.

Thus a nonzero row vector survives the upward map. Positive semidefiniteness, which is automatic for an operator times its adjoint, would only yield λσ ≥ 0. Strict positivity is a genuine arithmetic input. The point-condition construction gets the local scalars from its linked isotropy and scalar hypotheses before calling the pairing theorem. 6.6Locating one target type

The source calls σ and π paired if there are f ∈ Mσ and v ∈ Vπ with ⟨v, Tf⟩ ≠ 0. Assume that the target subspaces span V, are pairwise orthogonal, and that for each σ at most one π can pair with it. The uniqueness property is the upward form of Howe duality in this argument. Definitions of pairing, uniqueness and orthogonality[213]

Choose nonzero f in Mσ. If every target component were orthogonal to Tf, their span would also be orthogonal to it. This would force ⟨Tf, Tf⟩ = 0, contrary to the Gram identity. Some π therefore pairs with σ. Now take any g in the same row subspace. A nonzero inner product of Tg with a different component would supply a second paired type, contrary to uniqueness. Since the orthogonal components span V, Tg lies in Vπ. The entire image T(Mσ) is a nonzero subspace of Vπ. This is the exact inclusion called thetaOf. Equality with the full target type is unnecessary. Image condition[214] component proof[215]

6.7Reading the parameter at a split place

The source works with a CM field, a totally imaginary quadratic extension of a totally real number field. At a finite place of the real field which splits into two places in the CM field, the relevant unitary groups have local descriptions by general linear groups. Write K for the local field at the chosen place. The source rank is r = k + m − 1 and the target rank is r + t. The rank data impose r + 5 ≤ t. In particular r < t, the inequality used in the local classification theorem. These are dimensions of underlying linear groups. This proves the normalized quotient used in the local factor calculation. For a general arithmetic matrix coefficient the result is multiplied by its value at the identity. 7The arithmetic balance

A bound for a centered prime sum can survive a surprisingly large error in a single arithmetic measurement. The proof takes measurements at many places and along a chain, then divides by their total weight. This chapter follows that division and accounts for each power of the scale that it costs.

7.1An identity before an estimate

Write H for the finite abelian group used to label the translations, E = (ℤ/2ℤ)² × H, and Φ for the subgroup whose first coordinate is zero. The character χC equals +1 on Φ and −1 on its complement. The index 0 in a sum over additive characters denotes the character identically equal to one. The map ℓ assigns a complex number to each character. At this stage it is input data. Its identification with logarithmic derivatives belongs to the arithmetic realization. The two halves[308] The sign character[309]

Choose a > 0, a translation τ ∈ H, weights wρ > 0 for ρ ∈ Φ, and an integer cutoff N ≥ a/wρ for every such ρ. The host data distinguish a prime d and a finite set S containing 2 and the auxiliary parameter q1, with d outside S. Outside S and d inertia is trivial. At primes of S, both inertia and the specified Frobenius element lie in Φ. At d, the inertia elements are exactly zero and the involution sgc0 = ((1,0),0). Inertia here records the local symmetries invisible on the residue field. Frobenius describes raising residues to the residue-field size. The source packages these assumptions as HostFactsS. Host hypotheses[310]

Write A for the weighted arithmetic count. To assign a weight to g outside Φ, pair it with ρ = ((1,1),0) + g + ((0,0),τ) inside Φ. At n = pi the weight is (a/n − wρ)+, where the subscript means the positive part. At an unramified prime the character sum is 2 if g equals the ith Frobenius power and zero otherwise. Its contribution is therefore twice log p times the weight when that power lies outside Φ. At a prime of S the Frobenius coset lies inside Φ and contributes zero. At d the inertia subgroup has order two, so averaging replaces 2 by 1 at each matching element outside Φ. Each such weight contributes log d times its value. These three calculations identify the count with the finite character expansion. Local counts and normalization[311] The three character sums[312]

For v = wρ the identity (a/n − v)+ = v(a/(v n) − 1)+ changes the scale to y = a/v. Terms beyond the cutoff vanish. Write Gψ(y) for the centered ramp. For a nontrivial ψ it sums the von Mangoldt weight, multiplied by the local character value and y/n − 1, over 1 ≤ n ≤ y, then adds y ℓ(ψ). For the trivial character it uses the centered zeta ramp. Substitution gives the following main term, where γ is Euler’s constant. The centered character ramp[313] Main term and remainder[314]

M = a log a − (1 + γ)a − (a/|Φ|) ∑ρ ∈ Φ log wρ + a ℓ(χC).

The trivial character gives the first three terms. For the other characters the centering contributes −a ℓ(ψ). Summing the conjugate phases over the complementary half of E kills the nonconstant characters except χC, whose sum is −|Φ|. This accounts for the plus sign. The pairing of the two halves permutes the weight indices, giving precisely the average of their logarithms. The remainder A − M is the same character average with centered ramps in the summands. This proves the analytic identity at fixed host data. Identifying the degrees, periods, heights and covolumes of the geometric construction with this particular M is an additional theorem. Balance identity and sign calculation[315] The identification consumed by the geometric estimate[316]

7.2Which characters survive?

Let A0 be a subgroup of H. For ψ a character of E, put Sψ = ∑u ∈ A₀ ψ(0, −u). Translation by any v ∈ A0 permutes this sum and multiplies it by ψ(0, −v). Thus the sum vanishes whenever one of these multipliers differs from one. Otherwise it equals |A0|. For e1(τ) = ((1,0),τ) and s ∈ A0, the corresponding shifted sum acquires the phase ψ(e1(τ)). Summing over s ∈ T2 ⊆ A0 and averaging over subgroup translations therefore contributes a density δ2/2 with δ2 = |T2|/|H|. The two in the denominator comes from |Φ| = 2|H|. Translation and density identities[317]

For example, take H = ℤ/4ℤ and A0 = {0, 2}. On H the four characters are ψj(h) = exp(2πijh/4) for j = 0, 1, 2, 3. Averaging ψj over A0 gives (1 + (−1)j)/2. The odd indices cancel and the even ones survive with value 1. If T2 contains one element, its contribution occupies one of the eight positions in Φ. The factor 1/8 comes from that count, independently of which surviving character is evaluated.

At a scale x ≥ 3, fix a loss ε > 0, a real sampling weight c with |c| ≤ 1, and a finite sample T ⊆ H. The survivors form the annihilator Ψ of A0. A further selection K ⊆ Ψ retains characters used in the target. For these the source imposes ψ(sgc0) = 1 and includes the trivial character. Among retained characters, a character trivial on all of H receives weight 1. The others receive c. Call these weights ωψ. For retained characters nontrivial on H, the sum over T of ψ(0,τ) differs from c|T| in norm by at most M0x−1+ε|T|, where M0 also bounds |Ψ|. The constants bounding ℓ on retained nontrivial and discarded characters are respectively K0 and CE log x. The sum of norms of the discarded centered ramps is denoted Σ. Orthogonality by itself leaves this last error to be paid. Weights, discarded sum and sampling assumptions[318]

7.3Dividing the error by the observed weight

Write n = |H|, t = |T|, v = |T2|, m for the length of the chain and b for its positive weight scale. At a translation τ the measurement uses an amplitude aτ with |aτ/b − x| ≤ 1. In the realized chain aE is the size parameter Dd.a, and the adjustable positive parameter k is real. For each subgroup translation, Err bounds the sum, over all t samples and m chain positions, of A − Re M. Weights and translated gaps[319]

For each subgroup translation u, the local comparison keeps the indices ((0,1),s + u) with s ∈ T2. The source calls these the thick indices. At those indices b ≤ w ≤ b + η + 1 with η ≥ 0. Replacing w by b changes the weighted ramp by at most 3(x + 1)(η + 1). At each other index in Φ, w ≤ 2b′. The parameters satisfy b′, X′ > 0 and b′X′ ≤ xb, so aτ/w ≥ X′/3. On this range assume ‖Gψ(y)‖ ≤ yθ with θ ≥ 0. Omitting that term costs at most (x + 1)bθ. With f = |Φ|, the normalized character sum multiplies the sum of these two allowances by at most 2f. The conditions 6f(x + 1)(η + 1) ≤ b/x and 2f(x + 1)θ ≤ 1/x give a total allowance of 2b/x per measurement. Termwise comparison[320] The two local cost conditions[321] Thick indices[322]

At the central scale define the signed real signal B = ∑ψ ∈ K ωψ Re Gψ(x) − Σ, where Σ = ∑ψ ∈ Ψ ∖ K ‖Gψ(x)‖. Also put Q = t m b. The estimate takes the form

Q (v/2n)(B − 4X) ≤ Err + 2Q/x,   X = x1/2+ε.

For positive observed weight Qv/(2n), direct division shows what an error costs. The upper bound for B is 4X + (2n/v)(Err/Q + 2/x). In the four-translation example v/(2n) = 1/8, so a unit of normalized error Err/Q increases the allowance by eight. A large negative B already satisfies the inequality. Its use later in the proof therefore requires the specific linear combinations of characters that recover the desired upper bound.

For each surviving character, the source bounds the real part of its phase-weighted sample sum from below, comparing each aτ/b with x. After summation the lower bound is t(B − 4X). Averaging the local upper bounds over the subgroup introduces the factor v/(2n). The signed lower and upper estimates then give the displayed inequality. The norms in Σ permit the discarded characters to contribute with either sign. Single-character lower bound[323] From translated gaps to a scalar inequality[324] Application of the scalar lemma[325]

Assume x ≥ 3, ε > 0, C ≥ 0, b > 0, n ≥ 1, 0 ≤ aE ≤ 2x b. The scalar size hypothesis bounds Err by xCε times the sum of four quantities. The right column gives each quotient after division by Q. Complete scalar hypotheses[326]

The leading scales are consequently x/m, xm/k, m, k/n². Balancing the first and third suggests m near √x. This heuristic by itself supplies neither admissible ranks nor densities. The size lemma actually assumes

x1/2−ε ≤ m ≤ x1/2+ε/2,   xm ≤ k ≤ n²x1/2−ε,

7.4Recovering the level sum

For a level Λ of order o, core_gm applies the preceding argument with c = 1/(3o + 1) and M0 = 4o. The hypotheses EAtH and CoreAtH supply the local character estimates and compatible chain data at the chosen scale. In particular eD + eL ≥ 0 and the error exponent C can be taken as eD + eL + 3. GΛ(x) ≤ x1/2+(eD+eL+7)ε.

The exponent applies to scales carrying the required data. A fixed ε allows thresholds depending on the level and constants, uniformly in the later choices of host and sample. 8Supplying the arithmetic hypotheses

The arithmetic estimate uses many fields and many primes. To control their total contribution, the proof bounds the lengths of cohomology groups on carefully chosen intervals. This is where one must keep track of which parameters have already been fixed when a field or window is chosen.

The three contributions · Tower generators · Descent · Selecting the interval · The degree-two bound · The plus bound · Trace congruences · The minus bound · Choosing both primes · The final window

8.1From Galois representations to window data

Over a CM field E, the row hypothesis applies to a regular algebraic, polarized cuspidal automorphic representation of positive rank a. A CM field is a totally imaginary quadratic extension of a totally real field. In this setting a polarization relates a representation to a twist of its conjugate dual. For each allowed ℓ-adic coefficient realization, the conclusion gives a representation of the absolute Galois group on an a-dimensional ℓ-adic vector space, a weight and Hodge–Tate weight data. Its package of requirements includes continuity, semisimplicity and prescribed local compatibility. The local theory uses both places above ℓ and places away from ℓ. The row theorem is invoked to produce the arithmetic window. Galois row hypotheses and conclusion[333] Construction from the row[334]

The separate chapter on the two theta lifts explains the Galois input. For the derivative estimate used on the geometric side, see the factorial gain and the mixed-coordinate correction. The estimate on cohomology below has different indices and quantifiers.

8.2What the good arithmetic window controls

One can first think of a degree-one cohomology class as a way of assigning a value to each symmetry. A cocycle satisfies c(gh) = c(g) + g·c(h). Two choices give the same class if they differ by g ↦ g·a − a. For the group of order two acting trivially on ℤ/4, the choice at its generator must double to zero. The two possibilities 0 and 2 give exactly two classes. In the arithmetic problem the group is a Galois group, the action includes a twist and one retains classes whose restrictions vanish at the specified places. This is the reason a kernel of a restriction map occurs below.

We measure a finite ℤℓ-module by its length. Filter it until each successive quotient has order ℓ. If there are d quotients, its order is ℓd. Both ℤ/ℓ² and (ℤ/ℓ)² have length two, although they require different numbers of generators. Later the tower estimate uses both quantities. Over a coefficient ring with residue field of size ℓf, each quotient instead contributes f to the base-ℓ logarithm of the order.

Fix a number field E and a rational prime ℓ. The coefficient module here is the discrete quotient ℚℓ/ℤℓ. A Tate twist changes the scalar by which Galois acts. If the ℓ-adic cyclotomic character is χcyc, the action on this quotient uses χcyc−j for the integer j in the window sum. With this action the cocycle rule above becomes c(gh) = c(g) + χcyc(g)−jc(h). Vanishing on restriction means the restricted cocycle becomes a coboundary.

The source uses the Galois group with ramification allowed in the specified set of primes above ℓ. The set S in LData is precisely the finite places dividing ℓ. One chooses a place of the algebraic closure above each member and restricts to the corresponding decomposition group. Write hℓ,j for the ℤℓ-module length of the subgroup Sha of these locally trivial degree-one classes. The related degree-two group has coefficients ℤℓ(j + 1). Thus the locally trivial subgroup within degree one is the intersection of the kernels of those local restriction maps. The length bounded by VVle is its ℤℓ-module length. Intersection of restriction kernels[335] Local data, twists and lengths[336] Maps to the global Galois group[337]

Given t and B, VVle demands finiteness of every hℓ,j for 1 ≤ j < t, for all allowed choices of closure and local data. For every finite set P of rational primes it also requires

∑ℓ ∈ P (log ℓ) ∑1 ≤ j < t hℓ,j ≤ B.

The field varies with a primitive character ψ, the height in a cyclotomic tower, and two auxiliary primes q,d. In a cyclotomic field containing the relevant roots of unity, IsChiField specifies the subgroup fixing E by the intersection of four conditions on the exponent of an automorphism: congruence to ±1 modulo 2e+2, ψ(a) = 1, and two quadratic-symbol conditions at q and d. For a fixed ψ and 0 < ε < 1/52, choose any integer function e(x) satisfying x2+8ε ≤ 2e(x) ≤ 2x2+8ε for all x ≥ 1. Then VWin supplies J ≥ 1 and a threshold X0. For every X beyond it and every admissible pair (q,d) at scale X1/J, there is Y ≥ X1/J with Y² ≤ X. Throughout [Y,Y²], every such field satisfies the length bound for t = ⌊x401⌋ and B = exp(xε/2). An admissible pair must obey the prime, congruence, divisibility and logarithmic size conditions of WinPair. Field, auxiliary primes and complete quantifiers[338]

8.3Splitting the obstruction by the action of conjugation

There is a different estimate for each of three parts of the cohomological sum. To see where they come from, fix a CM field in the construction, a twist index j and an odd prime ℓ. Complex conjugation on the CM field induces a linear involution c on the degree-one cohomology. Its action preserves the locally trivial subgroup. Put s = (−1)j. Because 2 is a unit in ℤℓ, every locally trivial class v has a decomposition

v = ½(v + scv) + ½(v − scv).

Applying c to the first summand multiplies it by s, and applying it to the second multiplies it by −s. Both still lie in the subgroup. A vector in both eigenspaces satisfies 2sv = 0, hence vanishes. The sum is direct, so the full module length equals the sum of its two eigenspace lengths. The name “plus” in the source means eigenvalue (−1)j; for odd j this is the −1 eigenspace. At ℓ = 2 the projectors involve a forbidden division, and the full module is estimated separately. Direct-sum construction[339] Conjugation and the two parities[340]

On the joint window there are bounds B2 on the sum of full lengths at ℓ = 2, and B+ and B− on the logarithmically weighted odd-prime sums of the two corresponding lengths. Each comes with finiteness for its twists and primes. Length additivity gives finiteness of the full group at odd primes as well. For any finite prime set, split off 2 if present, and add the two odd-prime inequalities term by term. This proves the bound B2 log 2 + B+ + B−. It explains why the factor log 2 appears only on the first term. Finiteness hypotheses and combination theorem[341]

8.4Putting the three estimates on one interval

Existence of two arbitrarily distant intervals separately would give no control of their intersection. The source instead constructs a window satisfying a specified condition IsBWindow, which includes a bound at 2 and bounds on certain layers of auxiliary prime towers. The plus estimate is proved on every window satisfying this condition, once the same prime pair is large enough. Choose the maximum of the two thresholds for X, and an upper bound for the finitely many forbidden-size parameters for the two primes. An interval supplied by the first theorem then satisfies the second theorem with the same endpoints, field and tower level. The minus estimate applies to the composite CM field without any further window choice. Definition of the common window[342] Quantifiers of the plus estimate[343] Joint window assembly[344]

Write NE for the conductor of the field, t for the twist cutoff and u = NEt. On the accepted window u ≥ 1 and log u ≤ 2xε/4. Indeed NE ≤ 2e+2Nψqd. Taking logarithms, the page bound and t ≤ x401 contribute at most a fixed constant plus a constant times log x; the pair satisfies log(qd) ≤ xε/4. The first terms are eventually absorbed in a second xε/4. With constants C,K fixed before x, the three bounds take the form

B2 = exp(x4ε/5),   B− ≤ K exp(8xε/4),
B+ = uC + C exp(x4ε/5).

For u ≥ 1, uC ≤ exp(2|C|xε/4). Every exponent on the right of the displayed estimates is o(xε) for fixed ε > 0. Beyond a common threshold each exponential is at most exp(xε/4), and the sum of the fixed nonnegative prefactors, including log 2 and absolute values for constants, is itself at most exp(xε/4). Their product proves the required exp(xε/2). This comparison is uniform over fields obeying the conductor bound. Conductor estimate[345] Minus contribution[346] Uniform error ceiling[347] Assembly for the chosen field[348]

The tower estimate uses a bound on degree-two cohomology, Poitou–Tate duality, local finiteness, local Tate duality and the Ferrero–Washington theorem. The plus contribution also uses separate representation counts. The following argument explains how the number of generators of a tower module controls the choice of the common interval. Inputs to the tower estimate[349] Use at twist cutoff exponent 401[350]

8.5What Ferrero–Washington supplies in this proof

A generator bound limits how many independent ℓ-adic directions can contribute to the growth of a cohomology group. The argument starts with the ideal class groups of the number fields in the finite layers of a cyclotomic tower, passes to a single module for the infinite tower, and then recovers the length at any chosen finite layer as a quotient of that module. The class group of a number field is the group of its nonzero fractional ideals modulo principal ideals.

Write Cl(L) for the ideal class group of a number field L, written additively. The number of independent characters of order ℓ depends on Cl(L)/ℓCl(L). For an abelian extension K/ℚ containing a primitive ℓth root of unity, or a primitive fourth root of unity at ℓ = 2, the statement called Published.FerreroWashington gives a single integer r such that

|Cl(K(μℓⁿ))/ℓCl(K(μℓⁿ))| ≤ ℓr   for every n ≥ 0.

Here μℓⁿ denotes the roots of unity of order dividing ℓn. The constant can depend on ℓ and K. The name Published occurs in the type of the result. The actual window proof passes the theorem FW.ferreroWashington, whose written body constructs r. Class-group statement[351] Construction of the exponent[352] Use by the window proof[350]

First work in the full cyclotomic fields L = ℚ(μfℓⁿ) for fixed f > 1 prime to ℓ. Let C = Cl(L), let J be complex conjugation, and write E = (1 − J)C. The source supplies a bound B0 for the index of ℓC + (1 − γ)C, for its chosen Galois element γ. It also supplies N and n0, independent of n, such that in the integral group ring (γ − 1)N belongs to the ideal generated by θ, 1 + J and ℓ for n ≥ n0. Here θ is the integral element thetaH, whose coefficients use one representative from each pair of opposite residues. Stickelberger annihilation gives θ(1 − J)C = 0. The source selects the smoothing integer 2fℓ + 1. Uniform group-ring relation[353] Uniform index bound[354] Stickelberger annihilation[355] Choice of parameter and cyclotomic cases[356]

Put T = 1 − γ. Multiply the relation by 1 − J. The θ term kills the class group, the 1 + J term disappears because J² = 1, and the last term has image inside ℓE. Hence TN kills V = E/ℓE. Each quotient TaV/Ta+1V is an image of V/TV. The map 1 − J in turn sends C/(ℓC + TC) onto V/TV. Multiplying the at most N quotient sizes gives |V| ≤ B0N. On the finite group E, the kernel and cokernel of multiplication by ℓ have the same order, so the same bound holds for |E[ℓ]|. Group-ring relation acting on the class group[357] Bound for a nilpotent endomorphism[358]

At odd ℓ a reflection inequality bounds |C/(ℓC + E)| by ℓ times the number of ℓ-torsion elements on which conjugation acts by −1. Each such element x lies in E, since (1 − J)(((ℓ + 1)/2)x) = x, with the integer scalar (ℓ + 1)/2. The remaining factor |(ℓC + E)/ℓC| is at most |E/ℓE|. The resulting bound is ℓB02N. At ℓ = 2 put C− = ker(1 + J). The separate sign estimate gives [C−∶E] ≤ (2φ(4f))N, where φ is Euler’s totient. On C[2], the map 1 − J has image in E[2] and kernel in C−[2]. The latter has order at most [C−∶E] |E[2]|. The source uses the looser uniform bound ([C−∶E] |E[2]|)². Reflection at odd primes[359] Odd-prime index product[360] Sign estimate at 2[361] Two-primary index bound[362]

To transfer either bound, denoted by B, to the abelian field K, use its inclusion in a cyclotomic field. The embedding lemma chooses f,D before n. For every K′ = K(μℓⁿ) it produces a full cyclotomic field L of conductor fℓm, with m ≥ n0 and [L∶K′] ≤ Dℓn₀. Restrict the unramified ℤ/ℓ-characters from K′ to L. The size of the restriction kernel is bounded by the subgroup index [L∶K′], and Artin reciprocity bounds its image by the number of class-group characters of L. Thus |Cl(K′)/ℓCl(K′)| ≤ Dℓn₀B. The written proof chooses this integer itself for r, since it is at most ℓr. The arithmetic inputs to this derivation include the group-ring relation, the uniform ambiguous-class index, Stickelberger annihilation, reflection and the sign estimate at 2. Their statements have the pinned suppliers above. Embedding and degree calculation[363] Restriction of class-group characters[364] Uniform transfer[352]

8.6From class-group characters to generators

Let U∞ be the kernel of the ℓ-adic cyclotomic character on the absolute Galois group, and put A = ℚℓ/ℤℓ. For an integer s ≥ 1, let Ds be the group of locally constant homomorphisms U∞ → A vanishing on its intersections with every inertia group and with each decomposition group above a prime dividing s. Define Xs = Homℤℓ(Ds, A). The earlier cokernel calculation uses s = ℓ. The generator proof starts at s = 1. Local conditions on the characters[365] Definition of the character module[366] Its ℤℓ-linear dual[367]

At the finite field K(μℓⁿ), n ≥ 2, class field theory pulls the class-group characters onto the everywhere unramified ℤ/ℓ-characters. Their number is bounded by the cardinality of Cl/ℓCl, since they factor through that finite vector space and its dual has the same dimension. At infinite level every such character extends to a finite level. The extension theorem first extends the locally constant homomorphism and then enforces the local conditions after moving higher. Compactness of the relevant sets of decomposition and inertia elements makes a single higher level suffice. The images under restriction from successive levels are nested and cover the infinite-level characters. Any ℓr + 1 distinct characters would therefore already occur together at one level, contradicting the finite bound. Adding the decomposition conditions for s can only reduce their number. Class characters at each layer[368] Extending the character and its local conditions[369] Nested union at infinite level[370] Comparison of local conditions[371]

Every element of Ds has ℓ-power order. Its domain is compact, so its locally constant image is finite, and every element of A is killed by a power of ℓ. Further, Ds[ℓ] has at most ℓr elements by the character bound and the identification A[ℓ] ≅ ℤ/ℓ. Embed this vector space in Ar using at most r coordinates. Each coordinate extends to all of Ds because A is divisible and hence injective over the principal ideal domain ℤℓ. Their joint map is still injective. Indeed a nonzero kernel element of order ℓk would yield a nonzero kernel element of order ℓ by multiplication by ℓk−1. Any map Ds → A now extends to Ar. Each endomorphism of A is scalar multiplication by an ℓ-adic integer, as seen by its compatible values on the cyclic groups A[ℓk]. The r extended coordinates thus generate Xs. This proves the precise generator conclusion used in the layer bound, a surjection ℤℓr → Xs. Torsion of the character module[372] Embedding from its order-ℓ subgroup[373] Producing the generators of the dual[374] Endomorphisms of ℚℓ/ℤℓ[375]

8.7One generator bound before choosing the two primes

At each odd ℓ the abelian field datum is fixed. The argument above works in any realization of that field and the source takes R = max(1, r) to meet the positivity hypothesis. At 2 the field varies with q,d. Fix the abelian base datum M of degree b, adjoin i with i² = −1, and obtain an exponent g from the class-group bound there. Adjoining the two quadratic fields specified by q and d gives a generator bound uniform in all prime pairs with q ≡ 3 mod 8, d ≡ 7 mod 16 and qd coprime to the modulus of M. Transport between field realizations[376] Fixed odd-prime bound[377] Quantifiers for the varying fields at 2[378]

R2 = 4(g + 6b).

Allow ramification at q and then at d in the larger space of mod-2 characters. Their inertia groups can be tested on at most 2b and 4b orbits respectively, by the two congruences. Evaluating on one tame inertia generator per representative gives at most two choices per orbit. Two characters with the same values differ by one from the previous space. Thus the character count is at most 2g+6b. Next pass to the subgroups corresponding to the two quadratic extensions. Each step at most squares the count. For an index-two subgroup, conjugation by an outside element induces an involution c on its characters. In characteristic 2, (1 + c)² = 0, so the image lies in its kernel, the invariant characters. The source bounds the number of invariants by the old character count. Evaluation on the square of the outside element records the obstruction to extending an invariant character, and the quotient character of the index-two subgroup records this bit after extension. Hence the number of all characters is at most the square of the old count. Two squarings give the displayed exponent. Restoring the unramified and splitting conditions selects a subgroup, so the same bound applies to the two tower modules X1 and X2. Orbit counts from the prime congruences[379] Testing on tame inertia[380] The invariant characters and the extension obstruction[381] Index-two bound[382] Two local steps and two squarings[383]

8.8Why restriction recovers the locally trivial classes

Fix a field F in one of these towers. Let G be its absolute Galois group, χ its cyclotomic character, U = ker χ, and e a nonzero integer. The coefficient module A = ℚℓ/ℤℓ carries the action ρ(g) = χ(g)−e. For a class in degree one, inflate to G and restrict a cocycle z to U. Since U acts trivially, z restricts to an additive character φ, and every coboundary restricts to zero. Conjugation of the cocycle identity gives φ(gug−1) = ρ(g)φ(u). Local triviality forces φ to vanish on inertia and on decomposition groups above ℓ, in each case after intersection with U. We will recover exactly the equivariant characters with these vanishing conditions. For injectivity, suppose φ = 0. The cocycle then factors through the cyclotomic quotient. In our fields this quotient is procyclic. Choose g whose image topologically generates it. The value χ(g)−e − 1 is nonzero. Indeed the cyclotomic degrees over a fixed number field grow without bound, whereas the ℓ-adic roots of a fixed nonzero power are finite. Multiplication by this nonzero scalar is surjective on A, so choose a with (ρ(g) − 1)a = z(g). Subtract its coboundary. The resulting cocycle vanishes on g, hence by the cocycle rule on all its powers, and by continuity on the quotient. This is where the condition e ≠ 0 enters. For surjectivity let φ be one of the equivariant characters. Write C for the closure of the powers of a lift of a cyclotomic generator. Its compact image surjects onto χ(G), so G = CU. The source proves that φ vanishes on C ∩ U. In group-theoretic terms the pro-ℓ part of the procyclic group C maps onto an infinite pro-ℓ group. That part is ℤℓ, and all its nonzero closed subgroups have finite index. Its kernel is therefore zero. The intersection has only prime-to-ℓ finite quotients, so its continuous characters into ℓ-primary torsion vanish. The code proves this vanishing directly by congruences in finite quotients. We may consequently define

z(cu) = ρ(c)φ(u),   c ∈ C,   u ∈ U.

Two decompositions differ by an element of the intersection, making the formula independent of the choice. Equivariance gives the cocycle identity on multiplying two decompositions. Continuity follows because C × U → G is a continuous surjection of compact Hausdorff spaces, hence a quotient map. Away from ℓ, inertia already lies in the cyclotomic kernel, where φ vanishes. Above ℓ, the restricted cocycle vanishes on the kernel of the local cyclotomic character. Its image on the decomposition group is open in ℤℓ×, and the allowed roots of unity give the same procyclic condition. The preceding generator argument therefore subtracts a local coboundary. Inflation from the group unramified outside ℓ now supplies a locally trivial class, whose restriction is φ. One exponent works simultaneously for all these choices. Tracing three numerical witnesses in the proof gives C = 150. The theorem returned to the window argument quantifies existentially over C.
